1324.title: Thirty days, then a year
1324.hook: mourning eases after thirty days; Kaddish continues for a parent
1324.howItsDone: After shiva, Jewish mourners keep shloshim, the thirty days from the burial: they return to work but avoid celebrations; for a parent the mourning continues through much of the year, with the mourner's Kaddish said in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shiva: seven days at home, and the mourner speaks first. Your line: sit with them. Today, what happens when the seven days are over.

The last chapter of the Torah. Moses climbs a mountain, looks out over the land he will never enter, and dies there. Below, the people grieve, and the text gives their grief a length. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the children of Israel "wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days". Then the days of weeping end. The very next line turns to Joshua, and the people listen to him. They don't forget Moses. They can't. But after thirty days, they get up and walk forward.
screen: `MOSES DIES ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THIRTY DAYS OF WEEPING.` → `THEN THEY WALK ON.`

segments.voice: Shloshim means thirty. Turn it four ways. First, the text. Moses is mourned for thirty days, and so, the book of Numbers says, is his brother Aaron. Jewish law reads those thirty days as a pattern for every mourner. Second, the steps. Shiva comes first, the low chair and the open door. When it ends, in some communities, the mourners walk together around the block, stepping back into the street for the first time. Through the rest of the thirty days they return to work and errands but hold back from parties and celebrations, and some don't cut their hair. Life starts again, quietly. Third, a parent. For other close relatives, formal mourning ends at thirty days. For a father or a mother, tradition keeps it going through much of the year, and the child says the mourner's Kaddish with a congregation, day after day. A parent, the tradition seems to say, takes longer to set down. Fourth, the shape of it. Grief here isn't a switch that turns off on a date. It's a set of doors, each a little wider than the last: the grave, the week, the month, the year. Nobody expects you to come through the first door already healed. They only expect you to keep coming, slowly, and they keep a place for you while you do.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS FOR MOSES.` · `UP FROM THE LOW CHAIR.` · `LONGER FOR A PARENT.` · `DOORS, NOT A SWITCH.` · then, large: `SLOWLY BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that changed for you lately, or still feels raw: a loss, a move, an ending. Ask gently where you are on the steps, still on the low chair, out walking around the block, back at work but not at the party yet, and know there's no wrong answer; if you pray, bring it into your prayer. And if a loss you're carrying ever feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
Shloshim. Thirty: the month after a death, when mourners return to life slowly, and for a parent the mourning goes on. Today's word.
Your line: slowly back. Grief keeps its own calendar, and that is allowed. Until tomorrow.

1325.title: Stones and candles
1325.hook: a stone left on a grave, and a candle each year on the yahrzeit
1325.howItsDone: Jewish visitors to a grave often leave a small stone on the headstone, and each year on the yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death, families light a memorial candle at home, and children say Kaddish for a parent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shloshim: thirty days, and for a parent, much of the year. Your line: slowly back. Today, the last lesson on the life cycle.

A Jewish cemetery on a weekday afternoon. No funeral. Just rows of headstones, and on top of some, small stones: a gray pebble, a chip of granite, a smooth one carried from a beach in someone's pocket. Nobody sells them at the gate. People bring them, or bend down and pick one up from the path. And across town, on a kitchen counter, a candle in a glass burns through an ordinary day, and nobody blows it out. Two small objects finish the life cycle.
screen: `SMALL STONES ON A HEADSTONE.` → `NOBODY SELLS THEM.` → `A CANDLE ON THE COUNTER.`

segments.voice: First, the stone. There's no single agreed reason; people give several. Flowers wilt, and a stone doesn't. A stone tells the family someone came, even if nobody saw. And behind it is an old picture: in Genesis, when Rachel dies on the road, "Jacob set up a pillar upon her grave." She was here, and she was loved. Second, the candle, which you met near the end of year three. Each year, on the anniversary of a death by the Hebrew calendar, families mark the yahrzeit, a Yiddish word for that day. A candle is lit at home and left to burn through the day. People often connect it to Proverbs: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." A small flame for a whole life. Third, what goes with it. On the yahrzeit, children say Kaddish for a parent, and some give to charity or study a little Torah in their memory. The dead are remembered by the living doing good. Fourth, the whole block. It began with the idea that a life has rituals. A baby welcomed at the door, a covenant, a daughter's name, a first haircut, honey on the letters. Coming of age. A match, a canopy, seven blessings, a broken glass, peace in the home. Then the holy society, plain wood, the tear, the shovel, seven days, thirty days. And now a pebble and a flame. From the first welcome to the last stone, nobody passes through a Jewish life alone.

And if missing someone ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

Your line: stones remember. Someone came, and someone still remembers. That closes the life cycle.

1326.title: The holy tongue
1326.hook: the language of Torah and prayer, revived for daily life
1326.howItsDone: Jews pray and read Torah in Hebrew, called the holy tongue; in Israel Hebrew is also the everyday spoken language, while some religious communities keep Hebrew for prayer and study and speak Yiddish at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pebble on a headstone and a candle on the yahrzeit. Your line: stones remember. That closed the life cycle; today a new block begins, Hebrew from the roots up.

A toddler in Jerusalem tugs at a sleeve and asks for juice. A bus driver calls out the next stop. A teenager types a text and deletes it. A cashier says have a good day. And on Shabbat morning, a few streets away, a reader stands at a Torah scroll and chants Genesis. Every one of them is speaking Hebrew. The letters on the scroll are the letters on the bus timetable. The language of the Torah scroll is the language of the grocery list.
screen: `JUICE, A BUS STOP, A TEXT.` → `A TORAH SCROLL ON SHABBAT.` → `ONE LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Ivrit means Hebrew. Turn it four ways. First, the name. In Genesis, a survivor runs to tell "Abram the Hebrew" that his nephew has been captured: Abram ha-Ivri. An old midrash plays with the word: ever can mean the other side, and the rabbis picture the whole world on one side and Abraham alone on the other. That's a reading, not a dictionary entry, but it has stuck. Second, the holy tongue. Tradition calls the Hebrew of the Torah and the prayer book lashon hakodesh. For a long stretch of history, Jews in many lands spoke other languages at home and in the market: Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic and more. Hebrew stayed alive in prayer, in study, in letters between scholars, in the blessing over bread. Third, the return. You met Ben-Yehuda, who insisted his family speak Hebrew every day, back in year three. In modern times a movement set out to speak Hebrew again at the breakfast table, to babies, about the weather. It worked: today it's the daily language of Israel, with words for buses and texting no prophet ever needed. Fourth, two views side by side. Some religious communities keep the holy tongue for holy things, praying in Hebrew and talking at home in Yiddish, so prayer words stay set apart. Others see everyday Hebrew as its own blessing: ordinary life spoken in the language of the Torah. Both take the language seriously; they protect it differently. For the rest of this block, you'll go inside it, letter by letter.

Trace it slowly in the air with your finger, three arms joined at the bottom, and say its sound softly on the out-breath: sh. If you pray, you'll meet this letter in the word shalom.

1327.title: Twenty-two letters
1327.hook: the Hebrew alphabet: twenty-two letters, all consonants
1327.howItsDone: Jewish children learn the twenty-two letters of the alef-bet, all consonants, and then the vowel marks; a Torah scroll is written without vowels, so readers prepare from a printed text before chanting from the scroll.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ivrit: Hebrew, chanted from the scroll and spoken at breakfast. Your line: the holy tongue. Today, the whole set of letters.

Open Psalm one hundred nineteen in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, and odd headings interrupt the poem. Aleph. A stretch of verses. Beth. Another stretch. Gimel. Daleth. A strange word over every section. In English it's easy to skip them. In Hebrew you can't, because in each section every line begins with that letter. The whole psalm walks through the alphabet, from the first letter to the last: a poem about loving the Torah, built out of the letters the Torah is written in.
screen: `PSALM 119, ODD HEADINGS.` → `ALEPH, BETH, GIMEL, DALETH.` → `A WALK THROUGH THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Alef-bet: the Hebrew alphabet, named for its first two letters, alef and bet. You first met it in year one, with the man who knew no prayers and said the letters instead. Turn it four ways. First, the count. Count that psalm's headings, from Aleph to Tav: there are twenty-two. Other poems in the Bible are built the same way, like the woman of valor at the end of Proverbs, each line starting with the next letter. The alphabet becomes a frame for praise. Second, all consonants. Every one of the twenty-two is a consonant; no letter is simply a vowel, the way a or e is in English. Vowels, when they're shown, are small dots and dashes under, over and beside the letters. Third, the scroll. A Torah scroll is written with the letters alone, no vowel marks at all. The reader has to know how the words sound, so a child preparing to read from the Torah practices from a printed book with the vowels in, then reads from the scroll without them. Fourth, why it matters. Some teachers picture the letters as a body and the vowels as the breath that moves it. On the parchment the breath is missing, and the reader brings it. Every time the Torah is read aloud, a living voice supplies what the ink can't.

segments.voice: You'll hear the twenty-two names once; say them after, softly, or just listen: alef, bet, gimel, dalet, hey, vav, zayin, chet, tet, yod, kaf, lamed, mem, nun, samech, ayin, pey, tsadi, kuf, resh, shin, tav. You don't need to remember them all; notice which one stuck, maybe the first, maybe shin from yesterday. If you pray, some of these sounds are already in your prayers.

1328.title: Right to left
1328.hook: Hebrew is read from right to left
1328.howItsDone: Hebrew is written and read from right to left, so Hebrew books and prayer books open from the right; children learning to read trace words from the right margin, often starting with familiar words like Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alef-bet: twenty-two consonants, and the reader brings the vowels. Your line: twenty-two letters. Today, which way those letters run.

Hand a Hebrew prayer book to someone who's never held one, and watch their hands. They open it the usual way and land on the last page. They flip, frown, flip again. Then someone leans over, smiling, and turns the whole book around. The spine goes on the right. The first page sits where an English book would end, and its first line starts at the right-hand margin. Nothing is backward. It's just facing the other way.
screen: `OPENED FROM THE WRONG END.` → `THE SPINE ON THE RIGHT.` → `THE LINE STARTS AT THE RIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Hebrew is written and read from right to left: the pen starts at the right margin and travels left, and the eye follows. Second, the book. Because each line runs leftward, the binding sits on the right and pages turn from left to right. A Hebrew book begins where an English one ends. Third, one word, slowly. Take the line you first met in your second week, said by tradition morning and night, from Deuteronomy: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew the first word is Shema, three letters. On the far right, shin, with its three arms. To its left, mem. Then ayin. Shin, mem, ayin: Shema. Read the other way, it falls apart. Fourth, why it matters for a beginner. Eyes trained left to right have to slow down here; they want to jump the wrong way. That slowness isn't a problem to fix. It's a doorway. You can't skim a language you read against your habits, and attention in prayer is something the rabbis prize. They call it kavanah. So let the eye start on the right, and let it take its time.

segments.voice: Rest a finger on the table and start at the right: draw shin, three small arms rising from a base, then mem to its left, a box open at the bottom left corner, then ayin, two short strokes meeting in a tail that drops below the line. Trace the same path once more, slowly, right to left, and say the word softly as you finish: Shema. If you pray, it's the word that opens the Shema.
Right to left. The way Hebrew runs: from the right margin, from the right side of the book, one slow word at a time. Today's word.
Your line: right to left. Slow eyes make room for attention. Same time tomorrow.

1329.title: Alef
1329.hook: a silent letter; the rabbis note the Ten Words begin with it (anochi)
1329.howItsDone: Jewish learners meet alef first, as a silent letter that carries its vowel; the rabbis teach that the Ten Commandments open with anochi, 'I am', which begins with alef.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that starts on the right, and Shema traced leftward. Your line: right to left. Today, the first letter, on the far right of the alef-bet.

A mountain wrapped in smoke. Thunder, lightning, the sound of a horn growing louder and louder. The people stand at the foot of Sinai, shaking. Then God speaks. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the first words are "I am the LORD thy God." In Hebrew the very first word is anochi, I am. And anochi begins with alef, the first letter of the alphabet, which on its own makes no sound at all. All that thunder, and the first word opens on a silent letter.
screen: `SMOKE, THUNDER, A HORN.` → `ANOCHI: I AM.` → `IT BEGINS WITH A SILENT LETTER.`

segments.voice: You met a small alef once, written small at the start of Leviticus; today, alef itself. First, the sound that isn't there. Alef has no sound of its own. It holds a place: whatever vowel is written with it, ah or eh or oh, that's what you hear. It's the open mouth before the word. Second, a midrash. The Torah's first word, bereshit, in the beginning, starts with bet, the second letter. So an old midrash has alef come before God and complain: I'm the first letter, and you began the world with bet? And God answers: wait. When I give the Torah at Sinai, I will begin with you. The Ten Words do open with anochi, with alef. The silent letter was saved for the moment of revelation. Third, later teachers. Some pushed the thought further: they asked what the people at Sinai could really bear to hear, and suggested that perhaps it was the alef alone, the silent opening before any word, and that was enough. It's a teaching, not a claim about history, but it gives silence an honored place at the mountain. Fourth, an ordinary day. Talk often rushes past the alef; people start speaking before they've finished listening. Alef sits at the head of the alphabet as a reminder that the breath before the word comes first. Before bet and every letter after it, there's a letter you can see and cannot hear.
screen: `A LETTER WITH NO SOUND.` · `ALEF'S COMPLAINT, GOD'S PROMISE.` · `PERHAPS ONLY THE ALEF.` · `THE BREATH BEFORE THE WORD.` · then, large: `ALEF IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: Let your mouth fall slightly open, the way it does just before a word, and stay right there at the opening without saying anything. When a thought arrives, let it pass like a sound in another room, and come back to the open mouth and the breath moving through it. If you pray, let this silence be the doorway into your prayer.
Alef. The first letter: silent on its own, the open mouth before the word, and the start of anochi at Sinai. Today's word.
Your line: alef is silent. Listening comes before the word. See you tomorrow at bet.

1330.title: Bet
1330.hook: bayit, a house; the letter that opens the Torah
1330.howItsDone: Jewish learners meet bet as the second letter, linked to bayit, house; the Torah opens with bereshit, which begins with bet, and a midrash reads the letter's shape, closed on three sides and open on one, as a lesson about where to look.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alef: the silent letter that opens the Ten Words at Sinai. Your line: alef is silent. Today, the second letter, and the end of the week.

"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The Torah's first line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation. In Hebrew the first word is bereshit, and its first letter isn't alef. It's bet, the second letter. Before the light, before the waters, there's this one small shape on the parchment: a flat roof, a floor, a wall on the right, and on the left, an opening. Squint, and it's a room with the door left open. The rabbis squinted.

segments.voice: First, the name. Say the letter's name and you're close to bayit, the Hebrew word for house. It's the bet in Beit Knesset, a synagogue, a house of gathering, and in Beit Lechem, Bethlehem, the house of bread. Second, the shape. The same midrash that gave alef its promise at Sinai asks why the world begins with bet, and answers with the shape. Bet is closed above, closed below, closed behind, and open only in the direction the line is going. So, the rabbis say, don't ask what is above the heavens, below the depths, or before the beginning. Start from here and look forward. Hebrew runs right to left, so bet's open side faces left, toward every word that comes after it. Third, a house. Some readers put the two thoughts together: a world that begins with a house is a world made to be lived in. Not a monument. A home, with its door facing what comes next. Fourth, the week just past: thirty days of slowly coming back, a stone and a candle, then the holy tongue, twenty-two letters, right to left, a silent alef, and now a house. Seven days that walked from the grave into the alphabet, and found, at its second letter, a place to live.

segments.voice: If you're at home, let your eyes move slowly around the room; if not, picture the room you'll sleep in tonight. Notice what's above you, what's under you, and the door, then rest your attention on the door, the open side, and let a question sit: what might come through it today? If you pray, bring your home into your prayer.
Bet. The second letter, close to bayit, house: closed on three sides, open toward what comes next, and the first letter of the Torah. Today's word.
Your line: bet is a house. Its open side faces what comes next. Rest well.
